name: Atulyanatheswarar Temple, Arakandanallur
deity: Shiva as Atulyanatheswarar, with the goddess Azhagiya Ponnazhagi
period: Ancient hill shrine sung in the Tevaram (7th century); Pallava origins, Chola growth, and later masonry of the Vijayanagara period
summary: Atulyanatheswarar is the hill shrine on the Thenpennai near Tirukkovilur, the old Araiyani Nallur of the Tevaram, remembered for Sambandar's hymn that threw open its closed doors and restored its worship.

sections.history: Arakandanallur, long known as Araiyani Nallur, stands on the northern bank of the Thenpennai river in the old Nadu Nadu country near Tirukkovilur. Its hill shrine has been a place of Shaiva worship since the seventh century, when the saints sang of Atulyanatheswarar in the Tevaram and made it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The sanctuary is old in its foundations, with beginnings traced to the Pallavas and growth under the Cholas, while much of the masonry seen today belongs to the Vijayanagara age. Set upon its granite rise above the river, it has kept its worship across these many hands and centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple climbs a granite hill and is entered beneath a seven-tiered gopuram, the sanctum of Atulyanatheswarar set upon the rock. Early rock-cut work attributed to the Pallavas survives in the hill, and the later enclosures, mandapas and tower reflect the Chola and Vijayanagara builders who followed. The goddess Azhagiya Ponnazhagi has her own shrine within the complex, and the Thenpennai river below serves as the temple's sacred tirtham. The climb and the river together give the place the air of an old hill sanctuary.
sections.legends: The story most dear to Arakandanallur is Sambandar's. When the saint came to the town he found the temple shut, its doors closed by people of another faith so that worship had ceased and the rituals had fallen silent. Standing before the barred sanctuary, Sambandar sang a hymn in praise of Atulyanatheswarar, and at his words the doors opened of themselves, and the worship of the Lord was restored. From this the temple keeps the memory of a Lord whose praise opens what is closed, and the hymn that reopened the shrine is cherished among its people.
sections.festivals: The ten-day Vaikasi Brahmotsavam in May or June is the great festival of the year, when the deities are taken in procession and the hill sees its largest gatherings. Maha Shivaratri in February or March and Tirukarthikai in November or December, with its lamps along the hill, are kept with devotion, and the monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Arakandanallur asks for a little climbing and rewards it. Come in the cool of the morning, make the ascent to the sanctum of Atulyanatheswarar on the rock, and pause at the shrine of the goddess Azhagiya Ponnazhagi. From the hill the Thenpennai and the fields of the old Araiyani Nallur open below, and many visitors pair the temple with nearby Tirukkovilur. Those who like a shrine with a story and a view will find both here, best in the quiet of early light or evening.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Arakandanallur lies in Villupuram district, close to Tirukkovilur and reached by road from Villupuram and Tiruvannamalai; Villupuram is the nearest major railway junction and Puducherry and Tiruchirappalli the nearest airports. Buses serve the town, and the temple stands on the hill at its edge.
